Bohr’s phenomenon for functions on
the Boolean cube

Andreas Defant Address:
Institut für Mathematik,
Carl von Ossietzky Universität,
26111 Oldenburg, Germany. Email address: defant@mathematik.uni-oldenburg.de , Mieczysław Mastyło Address:
Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Sciences,
Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań,
Poznań, Poland. Email address: mastylo@amu.edu.pl and Antonio Pérez Address:
Departamento de Matemáticas,
Universidad de Murcia,
30100 Espinardo (Murcia), Spain. Email address: antonio.perez7@um.es
Abstract.

We study the asymptotic decay of the Fourier spectrum of real functions f:{−1,1}N→ℝf\colon\{-1,1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} in the spirit of Bohr’s phenomenon from complex analysis. Every such function admits a canonical representation through its Fourier-Walsh expansion f⁡(x)=∑S⊂{1,…,N}f^​(S)​xS,f(x)=\sum_{S\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}\,, where xS=∏k∈Sxkx^{S}=\prod_{k\in S}x_{k}. Given a class ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions on the Boolean cube {−1,1}N\{-1,1\}^{N}, the Boolean radius of ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined to be the largest ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 such that ∑S|f^​(S)|​ρ|S|≤‖f‖∞\sum_{S}{|\widehat{f}(S)|\rho^{|S|}}\leq\|f\|_{\infty} for every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}. We give the precise asymptotic behaviour of the Boolean radius of several natural subclasses of functions on finite Boolean cubes, as e.g. the class of all real functions on {−1,1}N\{-1,1\}^{N}, the subclass made of all homogeneous functions or certain threshold functions. Compared with the classical complex situation subtle differences as well as striking parallels occur.

1. Introduction

Recent years show a remarkable increase of articles on Bohr’s phenomenon in complex analysis. A special feature is given by the so-called Bohr radii of holomorphic functions in several variables.

The main aim of this article is to start a parallel study for real functions f:{−1,1}N→ℝf\colon\{-1,1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} on the Boolean cube {−1,1}N\{-1,1\}^{N}. The analysis of this type of maps is of fundamental interest in theoretical computer sciences, social choice, combinatorics, graph theory, etc. We refer to the surveys of [15] and [17], or the more extensive book [16].

Bohr’s famous power series theorem from [5] states that for each d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} and all complex polynomials f⁡(z)=∑k=0dck​zkf(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_{k}z^{k}, z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} we have that

∑k=0d|ck|​13k≤‖f‖𝕋,\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{d}|c_{k}|\frac{1}{3^{k}}\leq\|f\|_{\mathbb{T}}\,,

where ‖f‖𝕋\|f\|_{\mathbb{T}} stands for the supremum norm on the torus 𝕋={z:|z|=1}\mathbb{T}=\{z\colon|z|=1\}. Moreover, the radius r=1/3r=1/3 is best possible. In terms of Fourier analysis this can be equivalently formulated as

(1) ∑k=0d|f^​(k)|​13k≤‖f‖𝕋,\sum_{k=0}^{d}|\widehat{f}(k)|\frac{1}{3^{k}}\leq\|f\|_{\mathbb{T}}\,,

where f^​(k)\widehat{f}(k) as usual denotes the kkth Fourier coefficient of ff as a function on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. The concept of a multidimensional Bohr radius was introduced by Boas and Khavinson in [4]: Given N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} the NNth Bohr radius KNK_{N} is the best (i.e. largest) 0<r<10<r<1 such that for every polynomial ff in NN complex variables we have

(2) ∑α∈ℕ0N|f^​(α)|​rα≤‖f‖𝕋N,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{N}}{|\widehat{f}(\alpha)|\,r^{\alpha}}\leq\|f\|_{\mathbb{T}^{N}}\,,

where now the α\alphath Fourier coefficient of ff is given by

f^​(α)=∫𝕋Nf⁡(w)​w−α​𝑑w\widehat{f}(\alpha)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{N}}f(w)w^{-\alpha}\,dw

(d​wdw is the normalized Lebesgue measure on the NN-dimensional torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N} and ‖f‖𝕋N\|f\|_{\mathbb{T}^{N}} denotes the supremum norm of ff on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N}). Obviously, K1=1/3K_{1}=1/3, but we note that for no other index NN the precise value of KNK_{N} is known. On the other hand, it was shown in [4] through probabilistic methods that

lim supN→∞Nlog⁡N​KN≤1,\limsup_{N\to\infty}\sqrt{\tfrac{N}{\log N}}\,K_{N}\,\leq 1\,,

and in [6] based on the hypercontractivity of the Bohnenblust-Hille inequality that

Nlog⁡N​KN≥12+o⁡(1).\sqrt{\tfrac{N}{\log N}}\,K_{N}\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+o(1).

Improving the techniques which lead to the preceding result the main result of [2] states that in fact

(3) limN→∞Nlog⁡N​KN=1.\displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt{\tfrac{N}{\log N}}\,K_{N}=1\,.

Note that this equality is basically a result on the asymptotic decay of Fourier spectrum (f^​(α))α∈ℕ0N(\widehat{f}(\alpha))_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{N}} of polynomials ff on the compact abelian group 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N} in high dimensions NN.

The main aim of this article is to study Bohr’s phenomenon replacing the NN-dimensional torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N} by the NN-dimensional Boolean cube {−1,1}N\{-1,1\}^{N} ({±1}N\{\pm 1\}^{N} for short). We can look at {±1}N\{\pm 1\}^{N} as a compact abelian group endowed with the coordinatewise product and the discrete topology (the Haar measure is then given by the normalized counting measure). This way, for every function f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} we have an integral or expectation given by

𝔼⁡[f]:=12N​∑x∈{±1}Nf⁡(x),\mathbb{E}\big[f\big]:=\frac{1}{2^{N}}\sum_{x\in\{\pm 1\}^{N}}{f(x)}\,,

and for every 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty the LpL_{p}-norm of ff is given by

(4) ‖f‖p=𝔼​[|f⁡(x)|p]1/p.\|f\|_{p}=\mathbb{E}\big[|f(x)|^{p}\big]^{1/p}.

The dual group of {±1}N\{\pm 1\}^{N} actually consists of the set of all Walsh functions χS:{±1}N→{±1}\chi_{S}:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\{\pm 1\} indexed on S⊂[N]:={n:1≤n≤N}S\subset[N]:=\{n\colon 1\leq n\leq N\} and defined as

χS​(x)=xS:=∏k∈Sxk(x∅:=1).\chi_{S}(x)=x^{S}:=\prod_{k\in S}x_{k}\quad\,\big(x^{\emptyset}:=1\big).

This let us associate to every function ff as above its Fourier-Walsh expansion

(5) f⁡(x)=∑S⊂[N]f^​(S)​xS,x∈{±1}N,f(x)=\sum_{S\subset[N]}{\widehat{f}(S)\,x^{S}},\quad\,x\in\{\pm 1\}^{N}\,,

where the Fourier coefficients are given by f^​(S)=𝔼⁡[f⋅χS]\widehat{f}(S)=\mathbb{E}\big[f\cdot\chi_{S}\big]. The degree of a nonzero ff is given by

deg⁡f=max⁡{|S|:f^​(S)≠0}.\deg f=\max\{|S|\colon\widehat{f}(S)\neq 0\}\,.

We moreover say that ff is dd-homogeneous whether f^​(S)=0\widehat{f}(S)=0 for all S⊂[N]S\subset[N] with |S|≠d|S|\neq d, and simply homogeneous if it is dd-homogeneous for some 0≤d≤N0\leq d\leq N. For f=0f=0 we agree to consider it as a 00-homogeneous or degree-00 function, like the rest of constant functions.

We introduce now the main definition of the paper.

Definition 1.1.

The Boolean radius of a function f:{±1}N→ℝf\colon\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the positive real number ρ=ρ⁡(f)\rho=\rho(f) satisfying

∑S⊂[N]|f^​(S)|​ρ|S|=‖f‖∞.\sum_{S\subset[N]}{|\widehat{f}(S)|\rho^{|S|}}=\|f\|_{\infty}.

In general, calculating the exact Boolean radius of a given function may be very complicated, as complicated as determining the Fourier coefficients. However it may be possible to give estimations when we know some feature of the function such as the number of variables on which it depends, the distribution of the Fourier spectrum (whether it is concentrated in low levels or in sets with the same cardinality) or the size of 𝔼⁡[f]\mathbb{E}[f] in relation to ‖f‖∞\|f\|_{\infty}. For that let us consider the following concept:

Definition 1.2.

Given a class ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions on the Boolean cube {±1}N\{\pm{1}\}^{N}, the Boolean radius of ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined as

ρ⁡(ℱ)=sup{ρ≥0:∑S⊂[N]|f^​(S)|​ρ|S|≤‖f‖∞​ for every ​f∈ℱ},\displaystyle\rho(\mathcal{F})=\sup{\Big\{\rho\geq 0\colon\sum_{S\subset[N]}{|\widehat{f}(S)|\rho^{|S|}}\leq\|f\|_{\infty}\,\mbox{ for every }f\in\mathcal{F}\Big\}}\,,

or equivalently

ρ⁡(ℱ)=inf{ρ⁡(f):f∈ℱ}.\displaystyle\rho(\mathcal{F})=\inf{\{\rho(f)\colon f\in\mathcal{F}\}}\,.

We are going to concentrate on the following five classes defined for N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, 0≤d≤N0\leq d\leq N and 0≤δ≤10\leq\delta\leq 1:

  1. ℬN\mathcal{B}^{N} := all functions f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},

  2. ℬ=dN\mathcal{B}^{N}_{=d} := all dd-homogeneous f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},

  3. ℬhomN\mathcal{B}_{\text{hom}}^{N} := all homogeneous f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},

  4. ℬ≤dN\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\leq d} := all f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} with deg⁡f≤d\deg f\leq d,

  5. ℬδN\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta} := all f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} satisfying |𝔼⁡[f]|≤(1−δ)​‖f‖∞|\mathbb{E}[f]|\leq(1-\delta)\|f\|_{\infty}.

In section 2, we prove that the Boolean radius of ℬN\mathcal{B}^{N} is given by the formula

ρ⁡(ℬN)=21/N−1=log⁡2N​(1+o⁡(1)).\rho(\mathcal{B}^{N})=2^{1/N}-1=\frac{\log 2}{N}\big(1+o(1)\big).

In section 3 we deal with the families of homogeneous functions ℬ=mN\mathcal{B}_{=m}^{N} and ℬhomN\mathcal{B}_{\text{hom}}^{N}. We first prove in Theorem 3.1 that for each 1≤m≤N1\leq m\leq N there exists CmC_{m} (independent of NN) such that

Cm−1​N12​m​(Nm)−12​m≤ρ⁡(ℬ=mN)≤Cm​N12​m​(Nm)−12​m,C_{m}^{-1}\,N^{\frac{1}{2m}}\binom{N}{m}^{-\frac{1}{2m}}\leq\rho(\mathcal{B}_{=m}^{N})\leq C_{m}\,\,N^{\frac{1}{2m}}\binom{N}{m}^{-\frac{1}{2m}},

where moreover limmCm=1\lim_{m}{C_{m}}=1. This means that for mm large, the previous estimation is asymptotically optimal. The proof for the lower bound relies on a recently proved (Bohnenblust-Hille type) inequality (9) while the upper estimate is based on probabilistic arguments (see Lemma 3.3). The fact that CmC_{m} converges to one is the key to prove

ρ⁡(ℬhomN)=log⁡NN​(1+o⁡(1)).\rho(\mathcal{B}_{\text{hom}}^{N})=\sqrt{\frac{\log{N}}{N}}(1+o(1)).

(see Theorem 3.2). In section 4 we deal with the case of function of degree dd. Here the estimation for the Boolean radius of ℬ≤dN\mathcal{B}_{\leq d}^{N} is less accurate than the homogeneous case. We show in Theorem 4.1 that for each 1≤d≤N1\leq d\leq N there are constants cdc_{d} and CdC_{d} (independent of NN) such that

cd​1N12≤ρ⁡(ℬ≤dN)≤Cd​1Nd−12​d.c_{d}\frac{1}{N^{\frac{1}{2}}}\leq\rho(\mathcal{B}_{\leq d}^{N})\leq C_{d}\frac{1}{N^{\frac{d-1}{2d}}}.

The proof of the lower bound requires an inequality for functions on {±1}N\{\pm 1\}^{N} which might be of independent interest, namely that if f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a function of degree dd, then

(∑S≠∅|f^​(S)|2)12≤2​ed​(1−|f^​(∅)|).\Big(\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}{|\widehat{f}(S)|^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq 2e^{d}(1-|\widehat{f}(\emptyset)|).

The preparatory work for that reminds on inequalities of F. Wiener and Caratheodory for complex polynomials (see Corollaries 4.3 and 4.5 and the primal Theorem 4.2). Finally, the last section 5 is aimed to estimate the Boolean radius of ℬδN\mathcal{B}_{\delta}^{N}. The main result (see Theorem 5.1) shows that there is an absolute constant C>0C>0 such that for each N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and 12N≤δ≤1\frac{1}{2^{N}}\leq\delta\leq 1

C−1​1N​log⁡(2/δ)≤ρ⁡(ℬδN)≤C​1N​log⁡(2/δ).C^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}\sqrt{\log{(2/\delta)}}}\leq\rho(\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta})\leq C\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}\sqrt{\log{(2/\delta)}}}.

Note that δ=12N\delta=\frac{1}{2^{N}} is the smallest “sensitive” value since for all 0≤δ≤12N0\leq\delta\leq\frac{1}{2^{N}} we consequently have that

Ω⁡(1N)=ρ⁡(ℬN)≤ρ⁡(ℬδN)≤ρ⁡(ℬ1/2NN)=O⁡(1N).\Omega\Big(\frac{1}{N}\Big)=\rho(\mathcal{B}^{N})\leq\rho(\mathcal{B}_{\delta}^{N})\leq\rho(\mathcal{B}_{1/2^{N}}^{N})=O\Big(\frac{1}{N}\Big).

The proof of the lower estimation relies on the well-known hypercontractivity inequalities, while for the upper estimate we have to study the behaviour of the Boolean radius of the family of (threshold type) functions

ψα,N:{±1}N→ℝ,ψα,N​(x)=sign⁡(x1+…+xN−α),0≤α<N.\psi_{\alpha,N}:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\hskip 8.53581pt\psi_{\alpha,N}(x)=\sign{(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}-\alpha)},\hskip 8.53581pt0\leq\alpha<N.

Indeed, we prove in Theorem 5.4 that there is an absolute constant C>0C>0 such that

C−1​1α+N≤ρ⁡(ψα,N)≤C​1α+NC^{-1}\frac{1}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}\leq\rho(\psi_{\alpha,N})\leq C\frac{1}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}

for every 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N. The strategy of the proof actually allows to give the precise asymptotic decay of the Boolean radius of the majority function MajN=ψN,0\Maj_{N}=\psi_{N,0} for NN odd (Corollary 5.10).

2. Case 1: All functions on the Boolean cube

The following theorem gives the precise Boolean radius for all functions on the NN-dimensional Boolean cube {±1}N\{\pm{1}\}^{N}.

Theorem 2.1.

For each N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}

ρ⁡(ℬN)=21/N−1.\rho(\mathcal{B}_{N})=2^{1/N}-1.

In particular,

limN→∞N​ρ​(ℬN)=log⁡2.\lim_{N\to\infty}N\rho(\mathcal{B}_{N})=\log 2\,.

Let us compare this result with what we already explained in the introduction for polynomials f⁡(z)=∑α∈ℕ0Nf^​(α)​zαf(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{N}}\widehat{f}(\alpha)z^{\alpha} on the NN-dimensional torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N}. In the Boolean case we have the precise estimation of ρ⁡(ℬN)\rho(\mathcal{B}_{N}) for all NN, whether in the Bohr case this is only known for N=1N=1, namely K1=1/3K_{1}=1/3 (see again (1)). One of the key ingredients of Bohr’s original proof of (1) from [5] (more precisely the modification of Bohr’s proof by M. Riesz, I. Schur, and F. Wiener) is a result of F. Wiener which states that for every holomorphic function ff with Taylor coefficients cnc_{n} on the open unit disc 𝔻\mathbb{D} with ‖f‖∞≤1\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1 we have

(6) |cn|≤1−|c0|2≤2​(1−|c0|),n∈ℕ.|c_{n}|\leq 1-|c_{0}|^{2}\leq 2(1-|c_{0}|),\quad n\in\mathbb{N}\,.

The key point in the proof of Theorem 2.1 is that in the Boolean case we have a stronger F. Wiener type result as the following independently interesting lemma shows.

Lemma 2.2.

For every function f:{±1}N→[−1,1]f\colon\{\pm 1\}^{N}\to[-1,1] and each pair of subsets A,B⊂[N]A,B\subset[N] with A≠BA\neq B we have that

|f^​(A)|+|f^​(B)|≤1.\displaystyle|\widehat{f}(A)|+|\widehat{f}(B)|\leq 1.
Proof.

Without loss of generality we can assume that there exists k∈B∖Ak\in B\setminus A. Then, for each x∈{±1}Nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} we have

f⁡(x1,…,xk,…,xN)=∑S⊂[N]∖{k}f^​(S)​xS+∑S⊂[N],k∈Sf^​(S)​xSf(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},\ldots,x_{N})=\sum_{S\subset[N]\setminus\{k\}}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}+\sum_{S\subset[N],\,k\in S}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}

and

f⁡(x1,…,−xk,…,xN)=∑S⊂[N]∖{k}f^​(S)​xS−∑S⊂[N],k∈Sf^​(S)​xSf(x_{1},\ldots,-x_{k},\ldots,x_{N})=\sum_{S\subset[N]\setminus\{k\}}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}-\sum_{S\subset[N],\,k\in S}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}

Since ‖f‖∞≤1\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1, both equalities combined yield to

|∑S⊂[N]∖{k}f^​(S)​xS|+|∑S⊂[N],k∈Sf^​(S)​xS|≤1\Big|\sum_{S\subset[N]\setminus\{k\}}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}\Big|+\Big|\sum_{S\subset[N],\,k\in S}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}\Big|\leq 1

and so the claim follows by

|f^​(A)|+|f^​(B)|≤𝔼​|∑S⊂[N]∖{k}f^​(S)​xS|+𝔼|∑S⊂[N],k∈Sf^​(S)​xS|≤1.∎|\widehat{f}(A)|+|\widehat{f}(B)|\leq\mathbb{E}{\Big|\sum_{S\subset[N]\setminus\{k\}}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}\Big|}+\mathbb{E}{\Big|\sum_{S\subset[N],\,k\in S}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S}\Big|}\leq 1.\qed

We are ready to give the proof of the main result.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

Let f:{±1}N→ℝf\colon\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} with ‖f‖∞≤1\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1. Applying the estimate from Lemma 2.2, for every ρ>0\rho>0 we have

∑S⊂[N]|f^​(S)|​ρ|S|\displaystyle\sum_{S\subset[N]}{|\widehat{f}(S)|\rho^{|S|}} =|f^​(∅)|+∑S≠∅|f^​(S)|​ρ|S|\displaystyle=|\widehat{f}(\emptyset)|+\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}{|\widehat{f}(S)|\rho^{|S|}}
=|f^​(∅)|+(1−|f^​(∅)|)​∑k=1N(Nk)​ρk\displaystyle=|\widehat{f}(\emptyset)|+(1-|\widehat{f}(\emptyset)|)\sum_{k=1}^{N}\binom{N}{k}\rho^{k}
=|f^​(∅)|+(1−|f^​(∅)|)​((1+ρ)N−1).\displaystyle=|\widehat{f}(\emptyset)|+(1-|\widehat{f}(\emptyset)|)\big((1+\rho)^{N}-1\big).

If we put ρ=21/N−1\rho=2^{1/N}-1, then the last term is equal to 11 and so we conclude that ρ⁡(ℬN)≥21/N−1.\rho(\mathcal{B}_{N})\geq 2^{1/N}-1. Let us estimate now ρN\rho_{N} from above. We denote by 𝟏∈{±1}N\mathbf{1}\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} the element whose entries are all equal to 11. Now observe that the function F:{±1}N→{±1}F\colon\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\{\pm 1\} given by

F⁡(x)={−1,x=𝟏,1,x≠𝟏F(x)=\begin{cases}-1,\,&x=\mathbf{1},\\ 1,\,&x\neq\mathbf{1}\end{cases}

the Fourier expansion of FF is given by

F⁡(x)=1−12N−1+∑S≠∅−12N−1​xS,x∈{±1}N.F(x)=1-\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}+\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}{\frac{-1}{2^{N-1}}\,x^{S}},\quad\,x\in\{\pm 1\}^{N}.

To see this, note that the function f:{±1}N→ℝf\colon\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} given by f⁡(x)=1f(x)=1 for x=𝟏x=\mathbf{1} and f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0 for x≠𝟏x\neq\mathbf{1} has the following Fourier expansion

f⁡(x)=∏n=1N(1+xn2)=12N​∑S⊂[N]xS,x∈{±1}N.f(x)=\prod_{n=1}^{N}{\Big(\frac{1+x_{n}}{2}\Big)}=\frac{1}{2^{N}}\sum_{S\subset[N]}x^{S},\quad\,x\in\{\pm 1\}^{N}\,.

Since F⁡(x)=1−2​f​(x)F(x)=1-2f(x) for all x∈{±1}Nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{N}, the desired Fourier expansion for FF follows.

Finally, it follows from the definition of the Boolean radius ρN=ρ⁡(ℬN)\rho_{N}=\rho(\mathcal{B}_{N}) that

1=‖F‖∞≥1−12N−1+∑S≠∅12N−1​ρN|S|=1−12N−1+12N−1​((1+ρN)N−1).1=\|F\|_{\infty}\geq 1-\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}+\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}{\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}\rho_{N}^{|S|}}=1-\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}+\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}\big((1+\rho_{N})^{N}-1\big).

Thus, (1+ρN)N−1≤1(1+\rho_{N})^{N}-1\leq 1, and this proves that ρN=21/N−1\rho_{N}=2^{1/N}-1. ∎

3. Case 2: All homogeneous functions

The problem of estimating the Boolean radius of the classes ℬ=mN\mathcal{B}^{N}_{=m} and ℬhomN\mathcal{B}_{\text{hom}}^{N} of homogeneous functions on the Boolean cube {±1}N\{\pm{1}\}^{N} is more delicate than in the case of ℬN\mathcal{B}^{N}.

Theorem 3.1.

There is a constant C>1C>1 such that for each 1≤m≤N1\leq m\leq N

cm​N12​m​(Nm)−12​m≤ρ⁡(ℬ=mN)≤Cm​N12​m​(Nm)−12​m,c_{m}\,N^{\frac{1}{2m}}\binom{N}{m}^{\frac{-1}{2m}}\leq\rho(\mathcal{B}_{=m}^{N})\,\leq\,C_{m}N^{\frac{1}{2m}}\binom{N}{m}^{\frac{-1}{2m}}\,,

where

cm=1m12​m​Clog⁡mm and Cm=C1m.c_{m}=\frac{1}{m^{\frac{1}{2m}}C^{\sqrt{\frac{\log{m}}{m}}}}\quad\,\mbox{ and }\quad\,C_{m}=C^{\frac{1}{m}}.

Before we turn to consequences of this result and its proof, let us again compare with the analog results known for the NN-dimensional torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N} (instead of the Boolean cube {±1}N\{\pm 1\}^{N}). If we replace in (2) all polynomials by all mm-homogeneous polynomials and define the mmth Bohr radius KN=mK_{N}^{=m} as the best rr in this inequality, then it is implicitly proved in [2] and [6] that there is an absolute constant D>1D>1 which for all m,Nm,N satisfies

(7) 1D​(mN)m−12​m≤KN=m≤D​(mN)m−12​m.\frac{1}{D}\Big(\frac{m}{N}\Big)^{\frac{m-1}{2m}}\leq K_{N}^{=m}\leq D\Big(\frac{m}{N}\Big)^{\frac{m-1}{2m}}\,.

and hence for fixed mm the asymptotic decay of the Bohr radius KN=mK_{N}^{=m} and the Boolean radius ρ⁡(ℬ=mN)\rho(\mathcal{B}_{=m}^{N}) coincide.

The control of the decay of cmc_{m} and CmC_{m} as m→∞m\to\infty will give the following.

Corollary 3.2.
limN→∞Nlog⁡N​ρ​(ℬhomN)=1.\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt{\tfrac{N}{\log{N}}}\,\rho(\mathcal{B}_{{\rm{hom}}}^{N})=1\,.

Based on the above formula we come to the essential conclusion that the study of Boolean radii and Bohr radii show a remarkable difference. Indeed, note that

(8) limN→∞Nlog⁡N​KNhom=1,\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt{\tfrac{N}{\log{N}}}\,K_{N}^{\text{hom}}=1\,,

where the definition of KNhomK_{N}^{\text{hom}} just means to consider in (2) only homogeneous polynomials instead of all polynomials on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N} (see again [2] and [6]). So in case of polynomials on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N} Bohr radii do not distinguish between all polynomials (see (3)) and the homogeneous ones (see (8)). But in case of functions on {±1}N\{\pm 1\}^{N}, the preceding corollary and the result from Theorem 2.1 show a dramatic difference. The deeper reason for this difference is that the distortion between a function f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and its homogeneous parts

fm​(x)=∑S⊂[N],|S|=mf^​(S)​xS, 0≤m≤Nf_{m}(x)=\sum_{S\subset[N],|S|=m}\widehat{f}(S)x^{S},\quad\,0\leq m\leq N

becomes visible if we compare their supremum norms. We have that

‖fm‖∞≤Cm​‖f‖∞,\|f_{m}\|_{\infty}\leq C^{m}\|f\|_{\infty}\,,

where the best constant CC is at least ≥2\geq\sqrt{2} (see [7]), whereas by Cauchy inequalities the analog result for complex polynomials on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}^{N} allows a constant 11.

For the proofs of Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.2 we again need some preliminary results. The following inequality is a recent result from [7, Theorem 1.1], and we here state it for the sake of completeness: There is an absolute constant C>0C>0 such that for every function f:{±1}N→ℝf\colon\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} of degree dd we have that

(9) (∑|S|≤d|f^​(S)|2​dd+1)d+12​d≤Cd​log⁡d​‖f‖∞.\big(\sum_{|S|\leq d}{|\widehat{f}(S)|^{\frac{2d}{d+1}}}\big)^{\frac{d+1}{2d}}\leq C^{\sqrt{d\,\log{d}}}\|f\|_{\infty}.

The relevant feature for us is that the constant involved has subexponential growth in the sense that

limd→∞(Cd​log⁡d)1d=1,\lim_{d\to\infty}{\big(C^{\sqrt{d\log{d}}}\big)^{\frac{1}{d}}}=1,

which will play a fundamental role in the proof of Theorem 3.2. The second result is of probabilistic nature. In fact, it is a consequence of a celebrated result, and it will be crucial to estimate ρ⁡(ℬmN)\rho(\mathcal{B}_{m}^{N}) from above.

∑0<|S|≤N|f^​(S)|​ρ|S|\displaystyle\sum_{0<|S|\leq N}{|\widehat{f}(S)|\rho^{|S|}} ≤∑m=1N(∑|S|=m|f^​(S)|2​mm+1)m+12​m​ρm​(Nm)m−12​m\displaystyle\leq\sum_{m=1}^{N}{\big(\sum_{|S|=m}{|\widehat{f}(S)|^{\frac{2m}{m+1}}}\big)^{\frac{m+1}{2m}}\rho^{m}\binom{N}{m}^{\frac{m-1}{2m}}}

5. Case 4: The class ℬδN\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta}

The main result of this final section reads as follows.

Theorem 5.1.

There is an absolute constant C>0C>0 such that for each N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and every 12N≤δ≤1\frac{1}{2^{N}}\leq\delta\leq 1 we have that

(26) C−1N​log⁡(2/δ)≤ρ⁡(ℬδN)≤CN​log⁡(2/δ).\frac{C^{-1}}{\sqrt{N}\sqrt{\log{(2/\delta)}}}\leq\rho(\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta})\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{N}\sqrt{\log{(2/\delta)}}}.

The proof of the theorem is separated into two parts. First we deal with the left-hand side inequality of (26), which is based on the use of the hypercontractivity inequalities of Bonami-Gross. Recall that for −1<ρ<1-1<\rho<1 the noise operator TρT_{\rho} assigns to every function f:{±1}N→ℝf:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} on the Boolean cube the map

Tρ​f:{±1}N⟶ℝ,Tρ​f​(x):=∑S⊂[N]f^​(S)​ρ|S|​xS.T_{\rho}f:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R},\quad\,T_{\rho}f(x):=\sum_{S\subset[N]}{\widehat{f}(S)\rho^{|S|}x^{S}}.

An important feature of this operator is presented in the next celebrated result.

Theorem 5.2 (Bonami-Gross).

For every 1≤p≤q≤∞1\leq p\leq q\leq\infty

(27) ‖Tρ​f‖q≤‖f‖pwhenever ρ≤p−1q−1.\|T_{\rho}f\|_{q}\leq\|f\|_{p}\quad\,\mbox{whenever $\rho\leq\sqrt{\frac{p-1}{q-1}}$}.

On the other hand, to prove the right-hand side inequality of (26) we are giving precise estimations of certain type of threshold functions belonging to ℬδN\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta}.

Threshold type functions

Finally, we are going to show that the estimation in Theorem 5.3 is somehow optimal. For that we give precise estimates of the Boolean radius of the following two-parametric functions:

ψN,α:{±1}N→{±1},ψN,α​(x)=sign⁡(x1+…+xN−α),\psi_{N,\alpha}:\{\pm 1\}^{N}\rightarrow\{\pm 1\},\hskip 8.53581pt\psi_{N,\alpha}(x)=\sign{(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}-\alpha)}\,,

where α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, and as usual sign⁡(y)=1\sign(y)=1 for y≥0y\geq 0 and −1-1 for y<0y<0. Different values of α\alpha may generate the same function. We will restrict to the case in which α≥0\alpha\geq 0. For some results we will also work assuming that N−αN-\alpha is an odd natural number. This way, we guarantee that different values of α\alpha lead to different functions and we also avoid that sign⁡(0)\sign(0) appears. Let us point out that the functions ψN,α\psi_{N,\alpha} belong to a wider class of functions known as linear threshold function (see [16, Chapter 5]). The aim is to show the following result.

Theorem 5.4.

For each N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N we have that

(31) C−1​1α+N≤ρ⁡(ψN,α)≤C​1α+N,C^{-1}\frac{1}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}\leq\rho(\psi_{N,\alpha})\leq C\frac{1}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}\,,

where CC is an absolute constant independent of α\alpha and NN.

The proof is involved and requires a series of preliminary results. We start with a technical estimate for the Boolean radius with some extra assumption on α\alpha. For N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} with 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N let G:ℝ+→ℝ+G\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} be the function given by

(32) G⁡(r):=supz∈𝕋|1+z​r|N+α−12​|1−z​r|N−α−12,r∈ℝ+,G(r):=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{T}}{|1+zr|^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{2}}|1-zr|^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}},\quad\,r\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\,,

and use it to define ℐ:ℝ+→ℝ+\mathcal{I}\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} by

(33) ℐ⁡(ρ)=∫0ρG⁡(r)​𝑑r,ρ∈ℝ+.\mathcal{I}(\rho)=\int_{0}^{\rho}G(r)\>dr,\quad\,\rho\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\,.

Before we state and prove the required preliminary result we define, following Guadarrama [10], the Bohr radius for the class 𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{N} of all complex polynomials of degree at most NN by

(34) RN:=sup{r>0:∑k=0N|ck(p)|rk≤∥p∥𝔻,p(z)=∑k=0Nck(p)zk,z∈𝔻}.R_{N}:=\sup\bigg\{r>0:\,\sum_{k=0}^{N}|c_{k}(p)|r^{k}\leq\|p\|_{\mathbb{D}},\,\,\,p(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}c_{k}(p)z^{k},\,\,z\in\mathbb{D}\bigg\}.

It was proved in [10] that there exist absolute constants c1c_{1}, c2>0c_{2}>0 such that for large enough NN,

13+c13N/2<RN<13+c2​log⁡NN.\frac{1}{3}+\frac{c_{1}}{3^{N/2}}<R_{N}<\frac{1}{3}+c_{2}\frac{\log N}{N}.

Dryanov and Fournier [8] proved the following remarkable estimate: For every polynomial p∈𝒫Np\in\mathcal{P}_{N}, p⁡(z)=∑k=0Nck​zkp(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}c_{k}z^{k} we have

|ck|≤2​cos⁡(π[Nk]+2)​(‖p‖𝔻−|c0|), 1≤k≤N,|c_{k}|\leq 2\cos\bigg(\frac{\pi}{[\frac{N}{k}]+2}\bigg)\big(\|p\|_{\mathbb{D}}-|c_{0}|\big),\quad\,1\leq k\leq N,

where as usual [Nk][\frac{N}{k}] denotes the integer part of Nk\frac{N}{k}. This estimations implies that the unique root tNt_{N} in (0,1](0,1] of the equation

satisfies 0<tN≤RN0<t_{N}\leq R_{N}. We refer to a remarkable Fournier’s article [9], where among others it is shown that in fact tN<RNt_{N}<R_{N} for each NN.

An immediate consequence of Theorem 5.5 is the following corollary.

Corollary 5.6.

For N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N such that N−αN-\alpha is odd let ρ=ρα,N\rho=\rho_{\alpha,N} be the Boolean radius of ψ=ψα,N\psi=\psi_{\alpha,N}. Then

(45) ℐ⁡(ρ)≤1N​(N−1N−α−12)​∑n≤N−α−12(Nn)≤13​ℐ​(3​ρ).\mathcal{I}(\rho)\leq\frac{1}{N\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}}\sum_{n\leq\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}{\binom{N}{n}}\leq\frac{1}{3}\,\mathcal{I}(3\rho)\,.

Since 13≤RN\frac{1}{3}\leq R_{N} and GG is a strictly increasing continuous function on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}, the function r↦ℐ⁡(r)/rr\mapsto\mathcal{I}(r)/r is increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty). In consequence

RN​ℐ​(ρRN)≤13​ℐ​(3​ρ),R_{N}\mathcal{I}\Big(\frac{\rho}{R_{N}}\Big)\leq\frac{1}{3}\,\mathcal{I}(3\rho)\,,

and so Theorem 5.5 applies. ∎

We now start to analyze (45). In order to control the combinatorial numbers appearing in (45) we need an auxiliary result from [13], and to state this result we introduce the function Y:[0,∞)→[0,∞)Y\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) defined by

(46) Y⁡(x)=e12​x2​∫x∞e−12​t2​𝑑t,x≥0.Y(x)=e^{\frac{1}{2}x^{2}}\int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-\frac{1}{2}t^{2}}\,dt,\quad\,x\geq 0.
Lemma 5.7.

For each N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and each 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N with N−αN-\alpha being an odd integer, there exists a real number 0≤cα,N≤π/20\leq c_{\alpha,N}\leq\sqrt{\pi/2} such that

∑n≤N−α−12(Nn)=N​(N−1N−α−12)​Y​(α+1N)​exp⁡(cα,NN).\sum_{n\leq\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}{\binom{N}{n}}=\sqrt{N}\,\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}\,Y\left(\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\right)\,\exp{\left(\frac{c_{\alpha,N}}{\sqrt{N}}\right)}\,.
Proof.

It is proved in [13] that given N≥1N\geq 1 and N/2≤k≤NN/2\leq k\leq N, we have that

(47) ∑j=kN(Nj)=N​(N−1N−k)​Y​(2​k−NN)​exp⁡(E⁡(k,N)N)\sum_{j=k}^{N}{\binom{N}{j}}=\sqrt{N}\,\binom{N-1}{N-k}\,Y\left(\frac{2k-N}{\sqrt{N}}\right)\,\exp{\left(\frac{E(k,N)}{\sqrt{N}}\right)}

for some real number

0≤E⁡(k,N)≤min⁡(π2,2​N2​k−N).0\leq E(k,N)\leq\min{\left(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}},\frac{2\sqrt{N}}{2k-N}\right)}.

The properties of the binomial coefficients yield that

∑n≤N−α−12(Nn)=∑n≤N−α−12(NN−n)=∑n=N+α+12N(Nn).\sum_{n\leq\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}{\binom{N}{n}}=\sum_{n\leq\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}{\binom{N}{N-n}}=\sum_{n=\frac{N+\alpha+1}{2}}^{N}{\binom{N}{n}}.

Therefore, replacing k=N+α+12k=\frac{N+\alpha+1}{2} in (47) we get the result. ∎

We finally need another technical result which sheds more light on the functions GG and ℐ\mathcal{I} which were defined in (32) and (33), and appeared in Lemma 5.5.

Lemma 5.8.

For 0≤α≤N−10\leq\alpha\leq N-1 we have

G⁡(r)={(1+r)N+α−12​(1−r)N−α−12,r∈[0,rα],(1+r2)N−12​(1+αN−1)N+α−14​(1−αN−1)N−α−14,r∈[rα,1]G(r)=\begin{cases}(1+r)^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{2}}(1-r)^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}&,\,\ r\in[0,r_{\alpha}],\\ (1+r^{2})^{\frac{N-1}{2}}\left(1+\frac{\alpha}{N-1}\right)^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{4}}\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{N-1}\right)^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{4}}&,\,\,r\in[r_{\alpha},1]\end{cases}

rα:=α(N−1)+(N−1)2−α2.r_{\alpha}:=\frac{\alpha}{(N-1)+\sqrt{(N-1)^{2}-\alpha^{2}}}\,.

Putting z=c+i​t∈𝕋z=c+it\in\mathbb{T} with c2+t2=1c^{2}+t^{2}=1 we can write

G⁡(r)=supt∈[−1,1](1+r2+2​r​t)N+α−14​(1+r2−2​r​t)N−α−14,r∈[0,1].G(r)=\sup_{t\in[-1,1]}{(1+r^{2}+2rt)^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{4}}(1+r^{2}-2rt)^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{4}}},\quad\,r\in[0,1].

To show the required formula for GG we define for a given r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1] the function gr:[−1,1]→ℝ+g_{r}\colon[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}_{+} by

(48) gr​(t)=(1+r2+2​r​t)N+α−14​(1+r2−2​r​t)N−α−14,t∈[−1,1].\displaystyle g_{r}(t)=(1+r^{2}+2rt)^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{4}}(1+r^{2}-2rt)^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{4}},\quad\,t\in[-1,1].

Calculus yields that the first derivative

gr′​(t)=r2​(N−1)​(1+r2+2​r​t)N+α−14−1​(1+r2−2​r​t)N−α−14−1​(tα,r−t),t∈(−1,1)g_{r}^{\prime}(t)=r^{2}(N-1)(1+r^{2}+2rt)^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{4}-1}(1+r^{2}-2rt)^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{4}-1}\left(t_{\alpha,r}-t\right),\quad\,t\in(-1,1)

where

tα,r:=α⁡(1+r2)2​r​(N−1).t_{\alpha,r}:=\frac{\alpha(1+r^{2})}{2r(N-1)}.

We now observe that tα,r≤1t_{\alpha,r}\leq 1 if and only if r∈[rα,1]r\in[r_{\alpha},1], and that grg_{r} attains the maximum at tα,rt_{\alpha,r}. Thus

G⁡(r)=gr​(tα,r)=(1+r2)N−12​(1+αN−1)N+α−14​(1−αN−1)N−α−14.G(r)=g_{r}(t_{\alpha,r})=(1+r^{2})^{\frac{N-1}{2}}\left(1+\frac{\alpha}{N-1}\right)^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{4}}\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{N-1}\right)^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{4}}.

In the case when r∈[0,rα]r\in[0,r_{\alpha}], then gg is increasing on [−1,1][-1,1] and so

G⁡(r)=g⁡(1)=(1+r)N+α−12​(1−r)N−α−12,G(r)=g(1)=(1+r)^{\frac{N+\alpha-1}{2}}(1-r)^{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}},

and this completes the proof. ∎

G⁡(3​ρ)\displaystyle G(3\rho) ≤(1+αN−1)α2​(1+9​ρ2)N−12≤exp⁡(α22​(N−1)+9​ρ2​N−12)\displaystyle\leq\left(1+\frac{\alpha}{N-1}\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(1+9\rho^{2})^{\frac{N-1}{2}}\leq\exp{\left(\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2(N-1)}+9\rho^{2}\frac{N-1}{2}\right)}

Let us focus now on the proof of Theorem 5.4. Using again the fact that YY is a decreasing function with Y⁡(x)≤1/xY(x)\leq 1/x on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}, it can be easily shown (see [13]) that

(52) x1+x2≤Y⁡(x)≤1xfor every x>0.\frac{x}{1+x^{2}}\leq Y(x)\leq\frac{1}{x}\,\quad\mbox{for every $x>0$}.

Note that these estimations are not accurate when xx goes to zero, as Y⁡(0)Y(0) is a well-defined positive real number.

Proof of Theorem 5.4.

Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N. We start with the following observations: using the monotonicity of YY we have for α≤N\alpha\leq\sqrt{N} the bounds

Y⁡(2)N≤1N​Y​(α+1N)≤Y⁡(0)N;\frac{Y(2)}{\sqrt{N}}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}Y\Big(\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)\leq\frac{Y(0)}{\sqrt{N}};

while for α≥N\alpha\geq\sqrt{N} we can use the estimations (52) to deduce that

1N+α+1≤α+1N+(α+1)2≤1N​Y​(α+1N)≤1α+1≤2α+N\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}+\alpha+1}\leq\frac{\alpha+1}{N+(\alpha+1)^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}Y\Big(\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)\leq\frac{1}{\alpha+1}\leq\frac{2}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}

We can summarize the above inequalities by saying that there exists an absolute constant C0>0C_{0}>0 (independent of α\alpha and NN) which satisfies

(53) C0−1α+N≤1N​Y​(α+1N)≤C0α+N.\frac{C_{0}^{-1}}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}Y\Big(\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)\leq\frac{C_{0}}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}.

We divide now the proof of the theorem into two cases.

Case 1: Assume that N−αN-\alpha is an odd natural number. Then by (52) and Proposition 5.9 there is an absolute constant C0>0C_{0}>0 such that

(54) C0−1​1α+N≤ρ⁡(ψα,N)≤C0​1α+N.C_{0}^{-1}\frac{1}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}\leq\rho(\psi_{\alpha,N})\leq C_{0}\,\frac{1}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}.

Case 2: Without any restriction on 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N, let 0≤n<N/20\leq n<N/2 be an integer such that α∈[N−2n−2,N−2n)\alpha\in[N-2n-2,N-2n). Note that for each x∈{±1}Nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} the sum x1+…+xNx_{1}+\ldots+x_{N} is equal to N−2​kN-2k for some integer kk. Thus, if α′∈[N−2n−2,N−2n)\alpha^{\prime}\in[N-2n-2,N-2n) then ψN,α=ψN,α′\psi_{N,\alpha}=\psi_{N,\alpha^{\prime}}. In particular this is true for α′=N−2​n−1\alpha^{\prime}=N-2n-1, which satisfies that N−α′N-\alpha^{\prime} is an odd natural number. We can apply then (54) to obtain that

C0−1​1α′+N≤ρ⁡(ψα,N)=ρ⁡(ψα′,N)≤C0​1α′+N.C_{0}^{-1}\,\frac{1}{\alpha^{\prime}+\sqrt{N}}\leq\rho(\psi_{\alpha,N})=\rho(\psi_{\alpha^{\prime},N})\leq C_{0}\,\frac{1}{\alpha^{\prime}+\sqrt{N}}.

Finally, using that |α−α′|≤1|\alpha-\alpha^{\prime}|\leq 1 we conclude the result. ∎

The argument in Proposition 5.5 can be refined for the Majority function MajN\Maj_{N} (NN odd) to give the precise estimation of its Boolean radius as NN goes to infinity.

Corollary 5.10.

The Boolean radius of the Majority function satisfies

ρ⁡(MajN)=γN​(1+o⁡(1)),\rho\big(\Maj_{N}\big)=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{N}}(1+o(1)),

where γ>0\gamma>0 is the only real number satisfying ∫0γeu22​𝑑u=π2\int_{0}^{\gamma}{e^{\frac{u^{2}}{2}}\>du}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}.

Proof.

In the case of the Majority function MajN=ψN,0\Maj_{N}=\psi_{N,0} where NN is odd, we have that replacing zz by r​iri in (36) and comparing the coefficients of rmr^{m} (m∈ℕ)(m\in\mathbb{N}) on both sides we get that

∑n=1N(N−1n−1)​|ψ^N​([n])|​rn−1=(N−1N−12)​12N−1​(1+r2)N−12.\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\binom{N-1}{n-1}|\widehat{\psi}_{N}([n])|r^{n-1}}=\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}(1+r^{2})^{\frac{N-1}{2}}.

Denote by ρN\rho_{N} the Boolean radius of ψN\psi_{N}. Then, integrating between 00 and ρN\rho_{N} in the previous expression and using that ψ^N​(∅)=0\widehat{\psi}_{N}(\emptyset)=0 we deduce that

1N=1N​∑n=1N(Nn)​|ψ^​([n])|​ρNn=(N−1N−12)​12N−1​∫0ρN(1+r2)N−12​𝑑r,\frac{1}{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\binom{N}{n}|\widehat{\psi}([n])|\rho_{N}^{n}}=\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2^{N-1}}\int_{0}^{\rho_{N}}{(1+r^{2})^{\frac{N-1}{2}}\>dr},

where the first equality is just the definition of Boolean radius. Using Stirling’s approximation formula and the change of variables r=u/Nr=u/\sqrt{N}, we obtain that if CN:=ρN​N/γC_{N}:=\rho_{N}\sqrt{N}/\gamma (where γ\gamma is as above), then

∫0CN​γ(1+u2N)N−12​𝑑u=1N​2N−1(N−1N−12)=π2​(1+o⁡(1)).\int_{0}^{C_{N}\gamma}{\Big(1+\frac{u^{2}}{N}\Big)^{\frac{N-1}{2}}\>du}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\frac{2^{N-1}}{\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-1}{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\big(1+o(1)\big).

Hence CNC_{N} is bounded. Using the inequalities (1+1x)x≤e≤(1+1x)x+1(1+\frac{1}{x})^{x}\leq e\leq(1+\frac{1}{x})^{x+1} valid for x>0x>0 we obtain that

∫0CN​γeu22​𝑑u=π2​(1+o⁡(1)).\int_{0}^{C_{N}\gamma}{e^{\frac{u^{2}}{2}}\>du}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\big(1+o(1)\big).

By the definition of γ\gamma it follows that

∫γCN​γeu22​𝑑u=o⁡(1).\int_{\gamma}^{C_{N}\gamma}{e^{\frac{u^{2}}{2}}\>du}=o(1).

The mean value theorem yields that CN=1+o⁡(1)C_{N}=1+o(1) as we wanted to prove. ∎

Upper bound

Finally, we come back to the proof of the upper estimate in Theorem 5.1. We need another auxiliary

Lemma 5.11.

For every 0≤α≤N0\leq\alpha\leq N we have that

(55) σ⁡(x1+…+xN>α)≥exp⁡[−6​(1+αN)2].\sigma(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}>\alpha)\geq\exp{\left[-6\Big(1+\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)^{2}\right]}\,.
Proof.

We are going to distinguish two cases. If α≥N/2\alpha\geq N/2 then we have the trivial bound

σ⁡(x1+…+xN>α)≥2−N≥exp⁡(−N)≥exp⁡[−6​(1+αN)2].\sigma(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}>\alpha)\geq 2^{-N}\geq\exp{(-N)}\geq\exp{\left[-6\Big(1+\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)^{2}\right]}.

Assume that α<N/2\alpha<N/2. By Lemma 5.7 we have that

σ⁡(x1+…+xN>α)=12N​∑n≥N−α−12(Nn)≥N2N​(N−1N−α−12)​Y​(α+1N).\sigma(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}>\alpha)=\frac{1}{2^{N}}\sum_{n\geq\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}{\binom{N}{n}}\geq\frac{\sqrt{N}}{2^{N}}\,\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}\,Y\Big(\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big).

To bound the combinatorial number in the last expression let us recall some established bounds for binomial coefficients. From [12, p. 58] we know that for each 0≤m≤n0\leq m\leq n

(2​nn−m)≥(2​nn)​exp⁡(−m2n−m+1)≥22​n−1n​exp⁡(−m2n−m+1),\binom{2n}{n-m}\geq\binom{2n}{n}\,\exp{\Big(\frac{-m^{2}}{n-m+1}\Big)}\geq\frac{2^{2n-1}}{\sqrt{n}}\,\exp{\Big(\frac{-m^{2}}{n-m+1}\Big)}\,,

where the last inequality is consequence of classical Stirling estimations. This yields that if NN is an odd number and α\alpha is as above, then

(N−1N−α−12)≥242NNexp(−α22​(N−α+1))≥242NNexp(−α2N,)\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\frac{2^{N}}{\sqrt{N}}\,\exp{\Big(\frac{-\alpha^{2}}{2(N-\alpha+1)}\Big)}\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\frac{2^{N}}{\sqrt{N}}\exp{\Big(-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{N}\,,\Big)}

where the last inequality follows from the hypothesis α≤N/2\alpha\leq N/2. If NN is even, then we can use the standard relations between binomial coefficients and the previous bound to get

(N−1N−α−12)≥(N−2N−α−12)≥24​2N−1N−1​exp⁡(−(α−1)2N−1).\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}\geq\binom{N-2}{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\frac{2^{N-1}}{\sqrt{N-1}}\exp{\Big(-\frac{(\alpha-1)^{2}}{N-1}\Big)}\,.

To avoid this distinction between NN odd or even, we can write the common lower bound

(N−1N−α−12)≥28​2NN​exp⁡(−2​α2N).\binom{N-1}{\frac{N-\alpha-1}{2}}\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}\,\frac{2^{N}}{\sqrt{N}}\,\exp{\Big(-\frac{2\alpha^{2}}{N}\Big)}.

Thus, we have that

(56) σ⁡(x1+…+xn>α)≥28​exp⁡(−2​α2N)​Y​(α+1N).\sigma(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{n}>\alpha)\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}\,\exp{\Big(-\frac{2\alpha^{2}}{N}\Big)}\,Y\Big(\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)\,.

To bound the last factor we simply turn to the original definition (46) of the function YY from which we easily obtain that

Y⁡(α+1N)\displaystyle Y\Big(\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big) =exp⁡((α+1)22​N)​∫α+1N∞e−t22​𝑑t\displaystyle=\exp{\Big(\frac{(\alpha+1)^{2}}{2N}\Big)}\int_{\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}}^{\infty}{e^{-\frac{t^{2}}{2}}\>dt}
≥exp⁡(α22​N)⋅∫α+1Nα+1N+1e−t22​𝑑t\displaystyle\geq\exp{\Big(\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2N}\Big)}\cdot\int_{\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}}^{\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}+1}{e^{-\frac{t^{2}}{2}}\>dt}
≥exp⁡(α22​N)​exp⁡[−12​(1+α+1N)2]\displaystyle\geq\exp{\Big(\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2N}\Big)}\exp{\Big[-\frac{1}{2}\Big(1+\frac{\alpha+1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)^{2}\Big]}
≥exp⁡(α22​N)​exp⁡[−2​(1+αN)2].\displaystyle\geq\exp{\Big(\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2N}\Big)}\exp{\Big[-2\Big(1+\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)^{2}\Big]}\,.

Applying this last estimation to (56) we conclude that

σ⁡(x1+…+xN>α)\displaystyle\sigma(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}>\alpha) ≥28​exp⁡(−3​α22​N)​exp​[−2​(1+αN)2]\displaystyle\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}\exp{\Big(-\frac{3\alpha^{2}}{2N}\Big)}\,\exp{\Big[-2\Big(1+\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)^{2}\Big]}
≥exp⁡[−6​(1+αN)2].\displaystyle\geq\exp{\Big[-6\Big(1+\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)^{2}\Big]}\,.

Proof of Theorem 5.1.

Let N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and 12N≤δ≤1\frac{1}{2^{N}}\leq\delta\leq 1. It has already been proved in Theorem 5.3 that

ρ⁡(ℬδN)≥15​N​log⁡(2/δ).\rho(\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta})\geq\frac{1}{5\sqrt{N}\sqrt{\log{(2/\delta)}}}.

To prove the upper bound, we will make use of the threshold functions ψα,N, 0≤α<N\psi_{\alpha,N},\,0\leq\alpha<N which were studied in the previous section. Recall that

|𝔼⁡[ψα,N]|=1−2​σ​(x1+…+xN>α)=[1−2​σ​(x1+…+xN>α)]​‖ψα,N‖∞.\big|\mathbb{E}[\psi_{\alpha,N}]\big|=1-2\sigma(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}>\alpha)=\big[1-2\sigma(x_{1}+\ldots+x_{N}>\alpha)\big]\,\|\psi_{\alpha,N}\|_{\infty}.

Then, by Lemma 5.11 we deduce that ψα,N∈ℬδN\psi_{\alpha,N}\in\mathcal{B}_{\delta}^{N} whenever

(57) (1+αN)2=log⁡(2/δ)6.\left(1+\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{2}=\frac{\log{(2/\delta)}}{6}.

If δ<2/e6\delta<2/e^{6}, then we can find 0≤α<N0\leq\alpha<N satisfying (57), so that

ρ⁡(ℬδN)≤ρ⁡(ψN,α)≤Cα+N=CN​(1+αN)=C​6N​log⁡(2/δ).\rho(\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta})\leq\rho(\psi_{N,\alpha})\leq\frac{C}{\alpha+\sqrt{N}}=\frac{C}{\sqrt{N}\Big(1+\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)}=\frac{C\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{N}\sqrt{\log{(2/\delta)}}}.

If δ≥2/e6\delta\geq 2/e^{6}, then, since ψN,0∈ℬδN\psi_{N,0}\in\mathcal{B}^{N}_{\delta} holds trivially, we immediately have that

ρ⁡(ℬδN)≤ρ⁡(ψN,0)≤O⁡(1N).∎\rho(\mathcal{B}_{\delta}^{N})\leq\rho(\psi_{N,0})\leq O\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\Big)\,.\qed
